articles.summary: A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history.
articles.body: A stunning upset in the Texas governor race and sweeping Democratic victories across the country threaten to curtail the biggest-ever spending boom in US history. That could disrupt a key growth engine for America’s economy. Come January, states controlled by Democrats who support expanding or extending AI construction moratoriums will account for 45% of America’s planned data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. A quarter of America’s planned AI infrastructure buildout is set to take place in Texas alone. That doesn’t mean half of America’s planned data centers are on hold. Demand for AI is off the charts. Donald Trump is still president, and he’s already waving around his veto hat. And Democratic governors couldn’t stop every data center from being constructed even if they wanted to. But Tuesday’s election nevertheless represents a paradigm shift that could alter the pace and path of America’s nonstop AI spending spree – an investment boom that has, according to ING economists, accounted for as much as a quarter of total US economic growth this year. Those economic benefits are already real, supporting thousands of jobs. And AI has the potential to revolutionize the way we work. But an AI data center slowdown could come with important silver linings. It could rein in unfettered growth that has contributed to rebounding inflation and led to widespread public antipathy toward the technology and the data centers that house it. It could also curtail some questionable business models that have raised serious skepticism on Wall Street. Tapping the brakes could ultimately put AI – and the US economy – on a more sustainable path. What’s $1 trillion between friends? AI infrastructure spending is expected to approach $1 trillion a year, every year, for the foreseeable future, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. As a percentage of America’s gross domestic product, that would outpace every other investment boom in modern US history – including the construction of the railroads. The outcome of Tuesday’s elections could slow that spending, with vast consequences for the thousands of jobs and massive amounts of economic development that AI supports. Democrats gained gubernatorial seats in Nevada, Georgia, Ohio and Texas, where candidates campaigned on tightening data center regulations. Proposals from the governors-elect include ending tax breaks, tightening climate and electricity restrictions and allowing local governments to impose their own moratoriums on data center construction. But Texas is the big kahuna. Wells Fargo estimates that for every 10% reduction in planned Texas data center capacity, Big Tech companies will reduce their AI infrastructure spending by a stunning 1.6% (a lot of money when you’re measuring spending in the trillions of dollars). State and local politicians have a lot of jurisdiction and sway over that spending: enough to change whether some projects get financed, said Mona Dajani, co-chair of Cooley’s infrastructure, energy and real estate practice. Hundreds of data center developments that are still awaiting permits, utility service or tax incentives could be particularly exposed, Dajani noted. But even active construction projects could be threatened. Texas law grandfathers in some projects’ permits, protecting them from future changes to local permitting requirements – but that doesn’t resolve state permitting changes or electrical service guarantees that Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa could vacate. The wait for approvals could add significant costs for AI companies, Dajani said: Interest, equipment commitments and utility expenses will all continue to accrue, even while a project is on ice. At some point, existing projects could stop being financially viable. If that happens, AI companies – who have already strained to build out data centers fast enough to meet their anticipated demand – may not be able to meet their explosive spending targets. “This is a rare case where state and local leaders have influence of geopolitical-level import,” said Harry Krejsa, director of studies at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology. Unsustainable growth Data centers aren’t exclusively a Democratic issue: Americans have displayed bipartisan consensus for putting guardrails around data center buildouts. Texas Republican Governor Greg Abbott had already imposed a data center moratorium that Hinojosa campaigned on extending until lawmakers establish stronger AI regulations. But Trump had railed against any attempts to stymie AI’s growth and spending, citing economic and national security – particularly in the high-stakes race against China. Many Republican politicians who may have otherwise supported AI regulations, including frameworks for data center construction, remained silent. Still, there’s evidence that the AI buildout could be on an unsustainable path. The United States had 5,427 data centers at the end of last year, according to Stanford University’s AI Index Report, and AI companies have announced plans for 3,969 new US data centers, according to Aterio, a data center research company. But only about 800 are under construction, and AI experts have raised doubts about the viability of many of the announced projects. If Tuesday’s election results trigger an investment slowdown, that could trim some of the industry’s fat. Example A: CoreWeave, a neocloud business that rents out computing capacity, recently projected such extensive losses that its bond yields surged to 15% – the danger zone. That was particularly troubling, because its expected return on investment was only around 9%. In other words, CoreWeave loses money on every single dollar it spends on expanding its data center capacity. Deep-pocketed hyperscalers – Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft – don’t have that problem. But their stocks have been slammed in recent weeks as investors grow impatient with what they view as an unsustainable amount of spending that may not return profits for years. A path forward “AI is catching a break here,” said Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM US. Brusuelas expects growth to slow from last quarter’s 3.4% pace to something closer to 2.4% if there is an AI slowdown. That’s still solid long-term growth. And America’s economy is massive and diverse. Investment that otherwise would have gone to data centers can go elsewhere. “It’s slowing, but it doesn’t mean we’re going to have a recession,” Brusuelas said. It also presents an opportunity for AI companies to get smart about their future AI data center rollouts – and get put on a more sustainable course. The helter-skelter approach to data center construction has resulted in significant amounts of money getting flushed down the toilet in unworkable projects – collateral damage from massive competition to be first and biggest. Data centers already face $200 billion in project delays, according to Mike Mathews, global digital infrastructure practice leader at risk adviser Marsh. A more rational, politically sensitive approach could create longer-term benefits for the communities that host the data centers and for the AI companies themselves. There’s precedent for that. In the previous decade, the Googles of the world built out data centers for the cloud computing revolution, promoting the fact that they’d be built sustainably with renewable energy – even before it was cost-effective to do that. A similar, community-based approach could provide AI companies with the compute they need and give them the political and social license to operate their data centers for the long haul. “Like the saying goes: If you want to go fast, you go it alone; if you want to go far you go together,” said Krejsa. “If you squander political license to operate at home, that’ll be a bigger impediment to remaining competitive with China.”

articles.title: The architecture of Viksit Bharat: Capital, sovereign tech, and structural reform at the TOI Ideas for India Summit 2026
articles.summary: India’s trajectory toward 2047 is no longer defined by abstract demographic projections, but by the hard-nosed structural mechanics of economic
articles.body: India’s trajectory toward 2047 is no longer defined by abstract demographic projections, but by the hard-nosed structural mechanics of economic self-reliance.At the second edition of the TOI Ideas for India 2047 summit, convened by The Times of India in association with Optum and powered by Pigeon; industry titans, policymakers, and strategic minds gathered in New Delhi for a series of high-level roundtables. To capture the comprehensive breadth of the summit's flagship discussions, the deliberations were officially codified in the Ideas for India 2026 Compendium, serving as a strategic playbook for the nation's economic stakeholders.] Rather than offering conventional platitudes, the deliberations cut straight to the core challenges of national scale: decoupling from foreign supply chains, rewriting the calculus of capital deployment, modernizing archaic legal frameworks, and weaponizing indigenous technology. As the summit feted seven exceptional innovators whose ground-level solutions bridge deep-tech defense and sustainable agriculture, the overarching consensus was clear: India’s ascent to a developed economy demands an aggressive, institutional overhaul of how the nation manufactures, governs, and innovates.The macro blueprint of sovereign tech, capital architecture, and industrial scaleThe opening dialogues established an uncompromising premise: sovereign technology and industrial autonomy are non-negotiable prerequisites for a $35-trillion economy. Getting the tone during the inaugural panel, Rohit Agarwal, Senior Vice-President - Transformation,Innovation, Enablement, at Optum Operations Global, emphasized that India’s greatest opportunity lies not merely in its vast population scale, but in the sheer number of problem-solvers it is capable of cultivating.Building on this vision, Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal framed national ambition through the lens of strategic insulation, pointing to monumental capital outlays—such as the Rs 76,000-crore Vadhavan Port and the Rs 70,000-crore shipbuilding revitalization package—as critical levers to eliminate India’s historic vulnerability to foreign transshipment hubs. Yet, infrastructure alone cannot bridge the deficit. Kular Systems Chairperson Geetanjali Kirloskar injected a sharp fiscal reality into the room, noting that India’s R&D expenditure languishes at a meager 0.65% of GDP. For Viksit Bharat to move from rhetoric to reality, capital must flood high-impact frontiers like semiconductors, advanced materials, and biotechnology.This recalibration of capital extends directly into corporate strategy and manufacturing. BCG India Head Rahul Jain argued that India’s unique geopolitical neutrality positions it as the premier alternative global manufacturing base, urging domestic industries to locally produce everything currently imported by leveraging newly minted free-trade agreements and scale efficiencies. However, financing this industrial renaissance requires abandoning conventional venture capital playbooks. OfBusiness and Oxyzo co-founder Asish Mohapatra delivered a blunt assessment to aspiring founders: chasing equity prematurely misses the mark. Instead, businesses must extract liquidity directly through operational cash flows, customer advances, and debt channels, where institutional liquidity runs twenty to thirty times deeper than equity. Complementing this macro view, Optum Global Senior VP, Operations, Surinder Singh argued that national productivity cannot remain the exclusive domain of corporate behemoths; true economic resilience requires deploying shared digital intelligence to rescue starved micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) from forecasting blind spots.Institutional modernization through judicial efficiency and resource securityEconomic momentum inevitably collides with foundational institutional friction, most notably within the country's legal and ecological architectures. South Delhi MP Bansuri Swaraj introduced a pragmatic blueprint for integrating artificial intelligence into governance, arguing for the deployment of AI to adjudicate documentary-heavy matters, such as cheque-bouncing disputes and rent-control cases, within days rather than months. By insisting on strict human appellate panels and erecting a firewall against AI involvement in personal liberty cases, Swaraj underscored a sophisticated approach to judicial automation. Furthermore, her proposal to implement digital tracking IDs for undertrials establishes a vital humanitarian baseline: that no citizen should languish in state custody merely due to administrative delays in filing bail.Ecological security runs parallel to governance reform. Kent RO Founder Mahesh Gupta addressed the compounding crisis of water contamination, highlighting that public infrastructure cannot single-handedly shoulder the emerging threat of microplastics infiltrating drinking water. The roundtable revealed that safeguarding the nation's water tables requires moving past state-dependent funding models. As Jal Shakti Minister C.R. Patil noted, monumental water conservation networks have been successfully engineered across the country with zero government capital, driven entirely by strategic community mobilization and corporate social responsibility (CSR) endowments.Human capital re-engineering and the ecosystem of grassroots innovationAs artificial intelligence and automation compress traditional corporate hierarchies, flattening entry-level hiring pyramids into diamond-shaped structures that prioritize human judgment over routine execution, the human capital paradigm is undergoing a seismic shift. Partner & Chief People and Culture Officer at GT Bharat Prashant Mehra and Stovekraft Founder & MD Rajendra Gandhi emphasized that industry can no longer afford to treat academic institutions as passive pipelines. Corporations are increasingly forced to co-design curricula during students' formative years, shifting the market valuation entirely away from static degrees and toward demonstrable, job-ready proficiencies in robotics, manufacturing supervision, and tech integration.This urgency extends directly into the creative and entrepreneurial trenches. Actor and cultural commentator Avinash Tiwary delivered a sobering critique of the domestic innovation ecosystem, observing that grassroots inventors in hubs like Hyderabad and Bengaluru frequently find their breakthroughs bottlenecked by a lack of laboratory access and institutional grants—effectively forcing Indian innovation to run on charity. Pointing to regional infrastructure models like Telangana’s T-Works, Tiwary and fellow panelists underscored that scaling indigenous capabilities, from edge-AI counter-drone swarms to agricultural-waste biodegradable packaging; requires robust, institutionalized prototyping sandboxes.The horizon toward 2047Ultimately, the deliberations at the TOI Ideas for India summit underscored that the architecture of a developed nation is not forged in a vacuum of solitary breakthroughs. It is constructed at the intersection of sovereign industrial policy, unyielding judicial reform, hyper-efficient capital allocation, and grassroots technological self-reliance. As these institutional threads converge, India’s transition to 2047 transitions from an aspirational milestone into an inevitable operational reality.Disclaimer: This article is part of a Brand Initiative, Ideas for India, by TOI in partnership with Optum.You use AI every day. articles.title: Musk bet big on keeping Texas red. What happens to his business empire now?
articles.summary: Elon Musk poured millions into the midterms to support Republican candidates, mostly in the Texas senate race. But it was Democrat upsets for governor and attorney general that could cause bigger problems for his Texas-based companies.
articles.body: Elon Musk poured nearly half a billion dollars into the midterms to support Republican candidates, most to help Ken Paxton defeat Democrat James Talarico in the Texas Senate race. Talarico won. But it was the other Democrat upsets in the state, for governor and attorney general, that could cause bigger problems for Musk and his Texas-based companies: rocket and AI company SpaceX and electric car maker Tesla. Not only will he likely face greater regulatory scrutiny, but both candidates took direct aim at Musk and his businesses while on the campaign trail. “It’s less about the blue wave on the Senate or House side,” said tech analyst Daniel Ives, a SpaceX and Tesla bull, about what Tuesday’s election results mean for Musk. “It’s more with the Texas governor.” Democrat Nathan Johnson, who is replacing Paxton as Texas attorney general, said in July that, if elected, he would investigate whether SpaceX’s Starlink service was unfairly awarded grants designed to expand rural broadband. The internet service is SpaceX’s most profitable unit. And Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who unseated incumbent Greg Abbott, made opposition to data centers a major plank of her campaign. She has vowed to put a moratorium on new data center construction. Both Tesla and SpaceX have banked their future success on their AI efforts. SpaceX is planning major investments in new data centers in the next year, including the massive Colossal 3 to be built just outside of Brownsville, Texas. Unlike a lot of artificial intelligence companies, SpaceX earns a profit from selling time on its servers and cloud platforms to other AI companies. Hinojosa’s proposed moratorium would be a critical blow to its plans. “I mean, those Texas data center plans are a key part of Musk’s ambitions,” Ives said. He said that’s why SpaceX and Tesla shares fell Wednesday, both dropping more than 3%, even as many other tech stocks rose. Musk, the world’s richest person with a net worth estimated at about $898 billion, likely won’t sweat the money he lost backing Republicans, or even Wednesday’s decline in value for his shares. The bigger issue for Musk is an increased level of scrutiny, which he noted on his social media platform, X, on Wednesday. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk wrote, referencing his ultimate ambitions. Experts say lifting and operating data centers in outer space still face many hurdles. But even if it was possible, SpaceX may have to take off from a spaceport in Louisiana if Texas moves to limit launches. SpaceX has faced public criticism for the operation of its spaceport, “Starbase,” on Texas’ Gulf Coast. Some residents near the launch facilities have long expressed worries about disruptive sonic booms — which can be as loud as gunshots and register as small earthquakes — and collectively filed a lawsuit this year. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment about the lawsuit. But Musk has previously downplayed sonic booms, saying in a 2022 post on X that “storms and hurricanes that are far more serious than Starship launches.” Those resident complaints, however, could find a more sympathetic ear from Hinojosa compared to Abbott. (Hinojosa’s campaign did not respond to questions from CNN about her position on the spaceport.) Tesla also has a big operation in Texas, and its driverless “robotaxis” only operate in four cities in Texas and three cities in Florida. For comparison, rival Waymo, a unit of Alphabet, operates in 15 cities across the country. Local governments decide which vehicles, self-driving or otherwise, are allowed on their roads. “It would it would be a big blow if robotaxis faced more regulation,” Ives said. Tesla hasn’t listed profits or losses for its robotaxi service. But Musk has made it clear that Tesla’s future is selling rides in its robotaxis, not car sales. And a large part of Tesla’s evaluation is the expectation that its robotaxi service will eventually operate nationwide, Ives said. Ives also says Hinojosa’s threat to the AI industry goes beyond just SpaceX. Texas is a key to US AI development. The state has the most planned data centers in the country, according to research firm Cleanview, and is second only to Virginia for the number open or under construction. “Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout which makes worries around the future of the datacenter buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors,” Ives said in a note to investors Wednesday. “SpaceX stock will be under pressure.”

articles.title: Trump effect: US-based Indian techies are returning, but to what? Harsh reality of steep salary cuts
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump’s immigration and visa crackdown, AI-led layoffs in the technology sector and rising uncertainty on H-1B visas and green card
articles.body: US President Donald Trump’s immigration and visa crackdown, AI-led layoffs in the technology sector and rising uncertainty on H-1B visas and green card backlog is prompting a hoard of Indians to return.But, life is not that rosy for these returnees in India. Professionals who have spent years working in the US are finding it difficult to secure comparable roles, match their previous salaries or negotiate compensation that reflects their overseas experience.Employers in India are also increasingly looking for specialised skills rather than treating international work experience as an advantage in itself.So, the important question then is: what are these techies returning to? Are there enough roles to absorb their talent? And, what about the salary levels?How many have returned?Data from Xpheno, a specialist staffing firm, shared with TOI suggests that in 2026, so far 12,900 professionals have returned. In 2025, 15,100 techies returned to India in the whole year. The number of people who are moving to the US has also taken a hit. In 2025 it stood at 21,200, but in 2026 so far only 14,800 have moved. If this trend continues, the number of returnees may exceed the count of talent moving to the US.Importantly, industry experts see this trend continuing into the next year as well, particularly with uncertainty around US immigration policies and the growing opportunities in India's technology ecosystem.Kamal Karanth, co-founder, Xpheno explains why the trend is likely to continue: Given the continuing challenges and developments around talent relevant programs & schemes like H1B, PERM and OPT, the return of US-based Indian techies will likely continue for the near-future.“The current trajectory of tech talent movement between India and US is set on a path where this year's returnees count will exceed previous year's count. It will not be surprising if H-1B linked developments drive the returnees count to surpass the count of outbound tech talent from India to the US. It is quite possible that we'll witness the first net positive year on the India-US talent corridor, where we gain more tech talent from the US than what we lose to them,” he tells TOI.However, Neeti Sharma, CEO, TeamLease Digital says this is not a reversal of talent movement.“People will continue to move in both directions. What we are seeing is a gradual rebalancing, with India becoming an increasingly attractive destination for experienced technology professionals,” she tells TOI.“With GCCs taking on product ownership, AI development and global technology mandates, professionals now have more compelling reasons to build their careers here,” she adds.What are the roles US tech returnees are getting in India?Techies returning from the US are getting into a wide range of tech and techno-functional roles across the board.According to Xpheno, some of the top roles the returnees have been getting into include: Software engineers, Senior software engineers, Project & program manager, Data engineers, Data analysts, Technical architects & consultants, Full stack engineers, DevOps specialists.Experts see a lot of interest in AI engineering, cloud, product development and technology leadership roles.Neeti Sharma of TeamLease Digital says that companies in India are increasingly giving people the responsibility to build products, own platforms and drive technology decisions.“In the US, many professionals may have been working in specialised roles within larger global teams. In India, particularly in GCCs, they are getting an opportunity to take on larger responsibilities and own outcomes end to end,” she says.According to Sharma, close to 2500 senior returnees from the US have been absorbed within the GCC segment. Nearly 44% of GCCs now have ownership of platforms, products, AI adoption and business-critical functions. This is changing the nature of technology jobs in India.The stark difference in salary levelsBut, the flood of talent returning to India is faced with a harsh reality. Salary figures in India are not as fat. This means settling for a job that pays far less than the one in the US.According to Kamal Karanth, salary packages vary widely based on multiple factors like enterprise context, role, location, pedigree of talent, scope of mandate, enterprise urgency, client-fit quotient etc.In fact, he believes that gone are the days when a US-returned tag would command a premium.“At an enterprise level conscious efforts are deployed to maintain parity in packages at a role, location and experience level. There are no special top up packages offered to returnees purely on grounds of geographic exposure anymore. If anything, the role's definition, scope of output and performance parameters may be elevated to go with a higher package,” he tells TOI.Kamal Karanth shares an illustration of the difference in a returnee's US package versus Indian package:A Full Stack engineer on H-1B would be in the $70,000 to $150,000 per annum range, with $150,000 being the maximum pay set for outliers. The average annual pay for this role and experience level on H-1B is $105,000 (Rs 1 crore equivalent). The annual package range for the same talent in India is in the $20,000 (Rs 19 lakh) to $32,000 (Rs 30 lakh) range for the Top 1% percentile by skill and experience level. The stark difference in salary levels is evident.“The returning talent, at the top 1 percentile, would have to prepare to accept offers at 1/3 or 1/4th their US equivalent value,” he says.Karanth believes that the friction point is often the steep package expectations the returning talent comes with.“Returnees expecting local compensation packages equivalent to their US packages find it difficult or impossible to engage on potential opportunities in India. Returnees whose package expectations are moderated to the Indian employer's bandwidth & budget stand a better chance of being picked from the hiring funnel. Employers in India no longer bend backwards to match overseas packages to attract overseas or returnee talent,” he says.Neeti Sharma on the other hand believes that some roles can still command a premium.“Within India, specialised technology roles, particularly AI, cloud and cybersecurity, command a significant premium. Broadly, in GCCs, entry-level salaries range from Rs 6-12 lakhs annually, mid-level roles from Rs 18-35 lakhs annually, and senior positions from Rs 45-90 lakhs annually,” she says.Leadership and niche AI roles can go much higher.“For someone returning from the US, the expectation has to be aligned with the Indian market. The opportunity is not necessarily to match US salaries, but to get a larger role, greater ownership and the opportunity to build something in India,” she says.What does the trend mean for India’s IT sector and existing talent base?The trend is a positive one for the Indian IT sector, but the existing talent pool in India will face higher competition for the same jobs.“Rise in techies returning, especially from advanced & market defining geographies like the US, is a direct positive enrichment of India's tech sector. For a sector whose raw material is manpower, the addition of experienced talent exposed to and trained in key client markets is a fast track to further sophistication, with global outlook and elevated capabilities,” says Kamal Karanth.Such returnee talent also often brings along expertise in new and emerging tech stacks and frameworks that can move enterprise services further up the value-chain.The job competition for local talent in India escalates when returnees calibrate their package expectations to local scales.“Returnees available on local packages are a strong competition and contenders for a role, as their profile and pedigree offer more value per dollar on ROI terms. In the new emerging GCCs focused verticals and tailored services from Indian IT Services, returnee expats have a definite edge compared to their local counterparts,” Karanth believes.From the growth prospects of the IT sector, people returning from the US bring experience of working on global products, managing large teams and handling complex technology programmes. This adds to the depth of leadership and specialised talent available in India.However, Neeti Sharma points out that the market is selective.“Companies are looking for specific skills and relevant experience, not just international exposure. AI, cloud, product engineering and cybersecurity are areas where demand is particularly strong,” she says.“For professionals already in India, there will be more competition, especially at the mid and senior levels. But it also raises the bar for the entire talent pool. India's technology workforce will benefit from this exchange of experience, and the need to continuously upgrade skills will become even more important,” she adds.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bharti Airtel net profit up 24% to Rs 10,710 crore
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharti Airtel Thursday reported a profit of Rs 10,710 crore this Q2, up 24% from Rs 8,651 crore in same period last fiscal.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharti Airtel Thursday reported a profit of Rs 10,710 crore this Q2, up 24% from Rs 8,651 crore in same period last fiscal. Its consolidated revenue from operations rose 16.7% to Rs 60,878 crore compared to Rs 52,145 crore in the year-ago Q2. The leading telecom player’s share price closed 0.2% down at Rs 2,062.05 Thursday on BSE when the broader market was up 2.6%. The company reported an industry leading mobile average revenue per user (ARPU) at Rs 271, up 5.8% from Rs 256 in last Q2.Bharti Airtel executive VC Gopal Vittal said: “We delivered another quarter of consistent performance with consolidated revenues of Rs 60,878 crore, increasing 4.0% QoQ, underscoring the strength of our diversified portfolio. Africa delivered a standout quarter with 6.7% QoQ constant currency revenue growth…. India business recorded strong revenue growth of 2.7% sequentially. India mobile delivered revenue growth of 3.4% QoQ, backed by our strategy of portfolio premiumisation and winning quality customers.”Airtel had 37.7 crore customers as on Sept 30, 2026, up 3.6% from 36.4 crore in the corresponding quarter last year. Its smartphone customer base stood at 30.5 crore, up about 1.9 crore on a YoY basis. By the end of this Q2, it had about 3.5 lakh network towers as compared to 3.4 lakh last Q2.“Our postpaid momentum remained strong with record high net customers additions of 12 lakh. We added 29 lakh smartphone data customers with continued improvement of our industry leading ARPU at Rs 271. The homes business saw (about) 6.8 lakh customer additions… Our new growth engines continue to gain momentum. Our investment in a strategic land parcel during the quarter marks another important step towards realising our ambition of building 1 GW of data centre capacity,” Vittal added.You use AI every day. articles.title: JetBlue raises checked-bag fee again to ‘help offset’ operating costs
articles.summary: Less than a year after raising its checked-bag fees, JetBlue is once again increasing those same charges for most travelers.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Less than a year after raising its checked-bag fees , JetBlue is once again increasing those same charges for most travelers.

The airline’s website now indicates that travelers who book flights after Nov. 3 will pay $50 to check their first bag on off-peak flights within the U.S., Latin America, the Caribbean or Canada. At peak times, that fee increases to $55. Want to check a second bag? That’s now $70 at off-peak times and $75 at peak.

But that’s only if customers pay for their checked bags at least 24 hours before departure. Travelers who check bags within 24 hours of takeoff will be charged $60 for their first bag during off-peak times, and $70 for peak flights. A second bag is $75 off-peak, and $85 peak.

The prices reflect a significant jump from JetBlue’s previous checked-bag fees, which were already increased months ago in late March. Before this week, the fee for the first checked bag started at $39 (or $49 off-peak) and a second bag started at $59 (or $69 at peak times).

As was the case in March, JetBlue cited rising costs of jet fuel as one reason for the increases.

“We’re adjusting checked bag fees to help offset rising fuel and operating costs. This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one,” a spokesperson for the airline wrote in an emailed statement.

JetBlue currently allows passengers one carry-on item, at no additional charge, as well as one personal item.

With the new fee structure in place, the company is encouraging passengers to add their checked bags to their bookings sooner rather than later, in order to avoid charges incurred for checking bags within 24 hours of the flight. The carrier also said JetBlue will continue to waive the fee for certain travelers — namely, those who belong to its status programs or sign up for its JetBlue-branded credit cards.

“JetBlue Plus, JetBlue Business and JetBlue Premier Cardmembers will continue to receive their first checked bag free for the primary Cardmember and up to three travel companions when using their card to book JetBlue flights,” reads the airline’s statement. “TrueBlue Mosaic members will also continue to enjoy one free checked bag for Mosaic 1, and two free checked bags for Mosaic 2, 3 and 4.”

The company isn’t alone in raising its checked-bag fees in 2026. Around the same time that JetBlue raised its fee in March — and amid rising oil prices since the start of the war in Iran — U.S. carriers including Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines and United Airlines all raised their checked-bag fees for the average traveler.

articles.title: JPMorgan says Fed Chair Kevin Warsh needs to spend more time with Congress to keep his gig
articles.summary: JPMorgan with some spicy words of wisdom to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh.
articles.body:
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh may want to restructure his calendar for 2027 to schedule one fewer call with the president and spend less time on executive-level thinking about which committee he wants to create next.

In place of all this, Warsh should spend more time walking the halls of Congress chatting up newly elected Democratic members of Congress if he doesn't want to be a one-term Fed chair, the team at JPMorgan said in a spicy new hot take.

"Chair Warsh's term as Fed chair ends in May 2030," JPMorgan strategist Michael Feroli said. "While there's another election between now and then, last night [Election Day] increased the odds his term will end with Democratic control of the Senate. Unless he wants to be a one-term chair, Warsh will need to spend less time looking out the window and more time walking the halls of Congress."

"In fact," Feroli added, "this was one of the few pieces of advice Powell publicly gave to his successor: 'Our window into democratic accountability is Congress. And it's not a passive burden for us to go to Congress and talk to people. It's an affirmative, regular obligation.'"

Warsh — appointed by President Trump — assumed the Fed chair position in May, and brought with him a grand plan to overhaul Fed policy.

He quickly made waves at his inaugural June FOMC meeting by slashing forward guidance and shortening the Fed's rate decision statement.

His first signature policy move came in September, when he orchestrated a 25 basis point interest rate hike to take the federal funds target range to 3.75% to 4%.

Following the Fed's October hold on interest rates, Warsh delivered a resolute message to global markets, vowing that the Fed will achieve its 2% price stability mandate with "no ifs, ands, or buts."

articles.title: US worker productivity surges in third quarter
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 5 () - US worker productivity grew faster than expected in the third quarter, depressing labor costs and supporting views that ‌the labor mar...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - US worker productivity grew faster than expected in the third quarter, depressing labor costs and supporting views that ‌the labor market was not a source of inflation.

Nonfarm productivity, ‌which measures hourly output per worker, increased at a 3.6% annualized rate last quarter after advancing ​by an upwardly revised 2.1% pace in the April-June quarter, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast productivity increasing at a 2.8% rate after a previously reported 1.4% growth pace ‌in the second quarter.

Productivity ⁠is volatile on a quarter-on-quarter basis. It grew at a 2.1% rate from a year ago. Economists and policymakers are ⁠hoping that an artificial intelligence spending blitz will translate into significant productivity gains.

Unit labor costs — the price of labor per single unit of output — fell at ​a 0.7% ​rate last quarter. That was the ​first decline since the second ‌quarter of 2025 and followed an upwardly revised 1.9% growth pace in the second quarter.

Economists had forecast labor costs rising at a 0.6% pace after growing at a previously reported 1.2% rate. Labor costs grew at a 2.4% rate from a year ago.

They followed on the heels of data last week ‌showing a moderate increase in the Employment ​Cost Index, the broadest measure of labor ​costs, in the third quarter.

Policymakers ​and economists have argued that the jobs market was not ‌a source of inflation. Benign wage ​inflation gives the ​Federal Reserve more latitude to focus on rising price pressures stemming from the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran.

The US central bank last week ​left its benchmark overnight ‌interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." ​Economists expect the Fed to raise borrowing costs in December.

(Reporting by ​Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

articles.title: Rising vet bills drive more Americans to pet insurance
articles.summary: The rising cost of veterinary care is pushing more Americans to buy pet insurance, as advances in animal medicine give owners access to new treatments.
articles.body: The rising cost of veterinary care is pushing more Americans to buy pet insurance, as advances in animal medicine give owners access to treatments that were uncommon or unavailable a decade ago. For Norwalk, Ohio-based Amanda Moore, 45, whose dog Tasha was diagnosed with mammary cancer, it meant surgery, chemotherapy and radiation treatment that ​has cost about $20,500 so far. Embrace Pet Insurance reimbursed more than $14,300, she said. Embrace Pet Insurance policies are underwritten by American Modern Insurance Group. Moore said ‌radiation treatment was quoted at roughly $3,000 to $10,000. Tasha was initially given about six months to live but is doing well more than a year after the treatments. “I would not have been able to afford to do a lot of this myself without having pet insurance,” Moore told Reuters. “It allowed me to make decisions based on what was medically best for Tasha rather than what I could afford.” About ​7 million pets, or more than 4% of US pets, were covered by insurance policies in 2025, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association, ​up 9% from the previous year and 76% from five years ago. It is becoming the fastest-growing property and casualty insurance business line, ⁠with premiums projected to rise 17% to $6.4 billion in 2026, according to Tim Zawacki, head of financial institutions research at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The rise has come as ​annual veterinary spending averaged about $560 last year, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association, while treatment costs for specialized cancer care, surgery, advanced diagnostics and chronic-condition management can run ​into thousands of dollars. Insurer Trupanion said its highest individual claim has exceeded $150,000. Veterinarian-service prices were 4.6% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Veterinarians and insurers said rising treatment costs, along with the growing availability of advanced tests and treatments, are encouraging more owners to buy pet insurance. Karen Hauer, a veterinarian with more than two decades of ​practice, said supplies, shipping, employee healthcare and labor all cost more. “Are some owners delaying or declining treatment because of cost? Absolutely,” she said. The expanding range of care and ​specialists, including oncologists, cardiologists and dermatologists, has driven up costs. “That sophistication improves outcomes and helps pets live longer, but it also raises the cost,” said American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jen ‌Quammen. Richard Goldstein, ⁠global chief medical officer at animal health company Zoetis said pets are now living about 1.5 to 1.7 times longer than they did four decades ago, increasing demand for treatment of chronic conditions and other age-related diseases. Treatments such as Zoetis’ Apoquel and Cytopoint have expanded options for environmental allergies, which affect up to 15% of dogs, Goldstein said. Zoetis launched Cytopoint for allergic skin disease in 2016 and later received US approvals for osteoarthritis treatment Solensia for cats in 2022 and Librela for dogs in 2023. Cytopoint injections can cost ​roughly $50 to $200 per treatment, while monthly Librela ​injections are estimated at about $65 to $250 depending ⁠on dog size, according to pricing guides published by Vety, MarketWatch and SpectrumCare. Zoetis did not provide treatment-cost ranges. Actual costs can vary significantly by veterinary clinic, pet size, dosage requirements and geography. Veterinary diagnostics company IDEXX Laboratories has introduced testing tools, including its Cancer ​Dx screening panel and inVue Dx cytology platform, helping veterinarians diagnose cancer and other conditions more quickly and accurately. Chemotherapy, 3D-printed prosthetics, ​minimally invasive surgery, wearable ⁠health monitors and portable diagnostic equipment are also driving spending. Insurers say premiums are rising because of the increase in veterinary costs. “Veterinary medicine can do more than ever before, which means there is more care worth financing,” said Katie Seawell, Trupanion’s chief marketing officer. Trupanion said net subscription pet additions rose nearly 40% in the second quarter from a year ago. Embrace ⁠Pet Insurance said ​its average claim rose 6.9% in the second quarter to $432 from a year earlier. It reimbursed policyholders $62.9 ​million during the quarter. Arizona-based Maribeth Roufus had sticker shock when she got the bill for her dog Pepita’s herniated disc: about $10,000. Insurance reimbursed $7,791.02 of Pepita’s $10,038.77 veterinary bill, leaving Roufus responsible for about $2,247.75 out of pocket. “Because I knew ​a surgery of this magnitude would be covered by my policy, I just said, save my sweet girl,” she said.

articles.body:
Rep. Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) said Wednesday that there is going to be a tough battle to end President Trump’s tariffs when Democrats take over Congress.

“The president’s policies, without any resistance from the Republicans, have directly led to increasing prices. Life is much less affordable under this president, starting with these tariffs,” Stanton told NewsNation’s Blake Burman on “The Hill.”

“These tariffs are illegal. They’re increasing prices on working-class families across the United States of America. And they’re increasing prices on our allies, hurting their economies as well. These tariffs have got to go. We’re going to have one hell of a donnybrook over ending these tariffs, which is making life so much more expensive,” the Arizona Democrat added.

Stanton’s comments follow a notable victory for Democrats in this year’s midterms. The party won both the House and Senate. It is projected to grow its caucus in the House from 214 members to 262 , while its Senate caucus is projected to grow from 47 members to 55 , according to Decision Desk HQ.

The Democrats’ victory came amid a challenging political environment for Republicans, with the GOP weighed down by issues like the unpopular war in Iran, Trump’s slumping approval ratings and concerns about the cost of living.

With their majorities in both the House and Senate, Democrats will most likely work to stymie Trump’s policy agenda, including his tariffs. The president’s tariff agenda during his second term has rattled global markets, strained relationships with allies and increased economic uncertainty.

Earlier this week , Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin said Democrats should take action to end Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war if they regained power following the midterm elections.

“I think the first thing they should do is repeal the tariffs that Donald Trump put in place,” Martin said.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

JB Pritzker (D) said Wednesday that Democrats should pass legislation to raise the federal minimum wage on the heels of their midterm victories. “Well, there’s an easy way to start. Let’s raise the minimum wage in the United States,” Pritzker told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, when she asked what Democrats in Congress should focus…
articles.body:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker (D) said Wednesday that Democrats should pass legislation to raise the federal minimum wage on the heels of their midterm victories .

“Well, there’s an easy way to start. Let’s raise the minimum wage in the United States,” Pritzker told CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, when she asked what Democrats in Congress should focus on.

The federal minimum wage is $7.25 per hour, equating to an annual salary of $15,080. The minimum wage last increased in 2009, when it rose from $6.55 per hour under the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2007 — which a Democratic Congress passed and former President George W. Bush signed into law.

Pritzker said Wednesday that Americans “can’t survive” on making $7.25 an hour, saying individuals “can’t raise a family” on that salary.

Raising the minimum wage was one of a slew of policy proposals Pritzker highlighted in his “Fighting for Illinois: Day One Agenda,” which he released on Wednesday .

The Illinois governor, who won reelection to a third term this week, called on Congress to pass legislation to provide universal healthcare and reform the country’s immigration system.

The potential 2028 presidential candidate , whose state has a minimum wage of $15 per hour, said he would “hope” President Trump would not veto Democratic-led measures to lower the cost of living.

“I would hope that he understands what the American people have said,” Pritzker told Collins. “But I can tell you, Democrats need to be very clear that we are sticking up for raising wages and lowering costs for American families.”

articles.title: MAGA media is grappling with GOP’s crushing defeat — and tiptoeing around Trump
articles.summary: On President Donald Trump’s favorite TV shows, there is none of the election denialism that characterized his 2020 loss. But there is a whole lot of disbelief — and some early signs of disagreement about the best path forward for the Republican Party.
articles.body: On President Donald Trump’s favorite TV shows, there is none of the election denialism that characterized his 2020 loss. But there is a whole lot of disbelief — and some early signs of disagreement about the best path forward for the Republican Party. On Wednesday night the banner on Jesse Watters’ Fox News show asked “HOW DID THIS HAPPEN?” while Watters offered his answers: “Ultimately the election turned on the Iran war and to a certain extent the trade war,” he said, calling it a “two-punch combo.” Watters said “corruption was also a motivator” and “the Epstein files left a bad taste in people’s mouths.” Watters didn’t drill into Trump’s responsibility for any of that, however. For the most part, right-wing commentators are handling the president and his ego with kid gloves, lest they anger the viewer-in-chief and his still-loyal base. Podcaster Ben Shapiro went further than most on Wednesday, first extolling Trump for being “totally impervious” to criticism, then saying “there is a thin line between being impervious to bad criticism and being totally out of touch.” Fox host Laura Ingraham also tiptoed around that out-of-touch concern. “To me, it’s pretty simple,” she said. Voters “want things to get cheaper, and they generally, I think, want things to kind of calm down. And they hate war. And I mean hate war. Especially if it means that they have to pay more.” After acknowledging the GOP’s losses, many right-wing programs and podcasts made a familiar pivot to denigrating Democrats, especially newly elected senators like James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed. Commentators called them “commies,” “crazy people” and dozens of other insults. On Fox’s “The Five,” Watters exclaimed, “They voted for Tala-freak-o, man! They voted for Abdul bluh-bluh-bluh-bluh-bluh Mohammed! No one can really wrap their head around that.” Commentators on other networks have had no trouble explaining it. But while those analysts have placed most of the blame for the midterm rebuke on the president himself, Trump-devoted TV hosts and influencers have faulted people around Trump for letting him down. This is a default setting for MAGA media: Trump can’t be wrong; he can only be wronged. The GOP “has failed to follow his leadership,” Blaine Holt, a retired Air Force brigadier general, said on Newsmax Wednesday night. On “The Five,” Emily Compagno blamed unproductive GOP lawmakers for causing a blue wave: For two years “Congress had the tools, they had the majorities, and they used none of that.” Watters’ guest Caroline Sunshine said that White House chief of staff Susie Wiles “needs to resign” because “her campaign skills have not translated to governing.” At times the MAGA media aversion to blaming Trump personally is taken to a comic extreme. Radio host Steve Deace was ridiculed on social media for blaming Trump’s staff for his bizarre construction site photo op on Wednesday afternoon. “Whoever thought it was a good idea after last night’s results to send the president out the next day to tout his ballroom should be fired and never work in politics again, and perhaps even in prison forever like on the moon,” Deace wrote. Numerous commenters responded and said it was obvious that Trump sent himself out to brag about the ballroom. On Fox Wednesday night, Trump ally Sean Hannity – who recently held his wedding rehearsal dinner at Mar-a-Lago so that Trump could attend – discouraged the GOP from “finger-pointing” about the party’s failures. Hannity’s new bride, Ainsley Earhardt, was similarly dismissive: “This is normal. This is what happens usually in a midterm,” she said Wednesday morning, even though political experts have pointed out that this year’s wipeout is the worst in decades. Ex-Fox host Tucker Carlson, who has become an outspoken Trump critic on the right, had a very different reaction to the results. He said on his podcast that it’s a necessary reckoning for the party and spent more than an hour talking through it. “This is the end of the Trump era,” Carlson said, evincing little regret. There’s been none of that talk on Fox. On Wednesday night Hannity repeatedly reassured his viewers that the Democrats in Congress would “overreach” and provoke “buyer’s remorse.” And Ingraham said Trump’s “greatest moments may lie ahead.”

articles.title: Four ways in which government can look to abolish LTCG tax for all class of investors; what SBI report says
articles.summary: The State Bank of India (SBI) in its recent research report has listed ways in which the government can look at doing away with the long term capital
articles.body: The State Bank of India (SBI) in its recent research report has listed ways in which the government can look at doing away with the long term capital gains (LTCG) tax without taking a major hit on its revenue collections.The stock market had generated returns of around 30% in the preceding financial year, leading foreign investors to book profits during FY25.The market situation has since changed considerably. SBI Research pointed out that the Nifty's average return over the past three years was only 0.5%, while foreign institutional investors had collectively withdrawn Rs 4.8 lakh crore from Indian markets.The potential impact on market activity is another important consideration for doing away with LTCG, it says.A complete removal of LTCG tax could encourage higher market turnover after a specified period, even if the STT rate remained unchanged. STT collections are currently estimated at around Rs 73,000 crore for FY27. These receipts could rise in the coming years even if changes to LTCG taxation are introduced gradually.How LTCG should be abolishedAccording to SBI Research, there are several possible ways to restructure LTCG taxation.First, the exemption limit could be revised to account for the expansion of the retail investor base. Rather than retaining a fixed threshold, currently set at Rs 1.25 lakh, the government could consider linking it to inflation. This would help ensure that the exemption keeps pace with rising prices.Second, investors holding assets for longer periods could receive more favourable tax treatment. For instance, LTCG tax could be reduced to zero for investments held for more than two to three years, compared with the current rate of 12.5% applicable to holdings of one to two years.Third, any review of LTCG taxation could be accompanied by an increase in the securities transaction tax (STT). A 50% increase in STT could generate additional revenue of around Rs 45,000 crore in FY28. Introducing a tiered LTCG tax structure could also bring in further revenue.Fourth, the government could consider allowing investors to defer LTCG tax on mutual fund redemptions in proportion to the proceeds reinvested in eligible equity mutual funds within 90 days. A similar approach is available for property sales. Such a provision could help investors move their money from mutual funds delivering lower returns to funds offering more reasonable returns.Revenue hit for governmentAccording to SBI Research, the government could do away with long-term capital gains tax for all categories of investors without majorly affecting its fiscal consolidation targets.The SBI report estimates a revenue loss of Rs 40,000-50,000 crore in FY28, if LTCG tax is abolished.SBI Research assessed that eliminating LTCG tax would result in a revenue shortfall equivalent to just 0.1-0.2% of GDP. It said the government could accommodate this impact without moving away from its fiscal glide path.The research report put LTCG tax collections at approximately Rs 1 lakh crore in FY26, with receipts expected to fall further to Rs 40,000-50,000 crore in FY27.The collection of Rs 1.3 lakh crore recorded in FY25, it said, was an exception rather than a reflection of the prevailing trend."We believe the government would be able to take this hit if hypothetically, the entire capital gains taxes were abolished," the report said.SBI Research had originally put forward the proposal to abolish LTCG tax in its October 12 edition of Ecowrap. It argued that removing the levy could help bring foreign capital back into Indian markets and improve investor confidence at a time when foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have been consistently withdrawing money from domestic equities.The report had also recommended offering favourable tax treatment to investments held for two to three years. Such a move, it said, could encourage investors to commit capital for longer periods and make Indian equities a more attractive destination for global funds.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tech stocks plunge on worries about AI and Democrats’ midterm landslide
articles.summary: Shares in technology companies dropped sharply, compounding recent declines and sparking concerns about the durability of artificial intelligence boom.
articles.body: Shares in technology companies dropped sharply Thursday, compounding recent declines and sparking concerns about the durability of an artificial intelligence boom that has driven much of recent U.S. economic growth. The tech-focused Nasdaq 100 index dropped more than 6% in midmorning trading, to its lowest level in five months. The S&P 500 also fell 3.5%, putting it on track for its worst day since April 2025, when President Donald Trump’s global tariffs rocked markets. The S&P 500’s drop erased nearly $2.5 trillion in wealth from the index. Memory and chip firms SanDisk, Western Digital, AMD, Seagate and Micron were the index’s biggest losers, all plunging around 10%. The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks more than just tech stocks, also entered “correction” territory on Thursday, which is when a stock or index declines at least 10%. Tech stocks have surged in recent years as excitement about artificial intelligence has fueled billions of dollars in investments in, and by, the companies that make chips and infrastructure necessary for its development and operation. Since Election Day 2024, the Nasdaq has surged almost 40%. But questions about whether AI will enable the kind of productivity necessary to generate returns on those investments have grown louder in recent months. Also contributing to losses were the commanding Democratic victories across the country in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Numerous Democrats who won races for governor, attorney general and Senate and House seats have pledged to slow or halt the construction of AI data centers. Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia were of particular concern, because they are all large data center markets. Major established cloud computing providers Alphabet, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft also fell, but less than the overall market declines. Elon Musk’s companies SpaceX and Tesla each slid around 10%, largely in response to the midterm results. Musk, the world’s first trillionaire, spent hundreds of millions to help elect Republican midterm candidates. Until Tuesday’s rout, he was seen as one of the largest potential beneficiaries of Republican victories. Now that voters have so resoundingly rejected the GOP, Musk and his companies face the prospect of tighter regulation and even potential investigations at both the state and federal levels. The sell-off was triggered by two lackluster earnings reports from major chipmakers, Qualcomm and Arm Holdings, which were released on Wednesday night. Both companies posted results that investors generally viewed as mixed. In early trading, the two companies led the Nasdaq indexes lower. Qualcomm tumbled 9%, while Arm Holdings slipped around 15%. Earnings reports like these have rattled investors in recent months because of the hundreds of billions of dollars that are being poured into the AI sector. Amid the sell-off Thursday, investors sought safer places for their money, sending the S&P 500’s consumer staples, health and utilities sectors higher. Oil prices rebounded from Wednesday’s drop. As of midmorning trading, Brent crude oil neared $100 per barrel again after falling below the key psychological level a day earlier. U.S. Treasury yields, which have faced some competition from tech giants tapping the bond markets to raise funds for their AI ambitions, were generally flat. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped nearly 700 points. The biggest contributor to the Dow’s drop was Nvidia, which sold off by 7%, its largest one-day decline since April 2025. Nvidia is the most important supplier to any AI firm, but as investors raise questions about returns, the euphoria in the industry is fading. Nvidia’s shares have tanked 15% over the past three months. Dow components Cisco and Caterpillar, which are both major suppliers to AI data centers, also dropped around 5%.

articles.title: Wealthy savers think they need $1.26 million to retire. They have half that.
articles.summary: Wealthy savers have only about half of their target retirement savings. Here's what the gap could mean for planning.
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

Retirement planning often starts with a savings target, such as $1 million or $2 million. However, whatever the goal, how much you need to fund your life after work will depend on priorities that are likely to change.

New research from HSBC pegs the amount affluent individuals believe they will need to retire at $1.26 million. Yet the investors surveyed have accumulated only half that amount, on average.

Closing the gap requires considering how your plans may be altered by new ambitions and responsibilities, experts say.

"The idea that life unfolds one stage at a time no longer matches reality," Lavanya Chari, head of wealth solutions and Premier Banking at HSBC, said in the report. "Retirement and legacy are moving into the middle of life, alongside caring responsibilities, financial commitments and ambitions such as a career change or pursuing a life goal."

HSBC surveyed 9,993 affluent and high-net-worth individuals aged 21 to 69, with investable assets ranging from $100,000 to $2 million.

The $1.26 million retirement savings target noted by respondents is 20% higher than the figure in HSBC's survey a year ago. Most respondents (71%) said they are planning for a "non-linear future" — funding two or three life stages, rather than just one.

"For generations, success followed a familiar sequence: one career, one home, marriage, children, then retirement," said Dacher Keltner, professor of psychology at UC Berkeley. "Over the next decade, these milestones will keep shifting and overlapping. Some may stop defining success at all. What seems unconventional today — multiple careers, extended families, and later-life reinvention — could soon become mainstream."

Margie Glenn, a certified public accountant and certified financial planner with Moneta Wealth Management in St. Louis, said she's seeing the same departure from the traditional path of working full time, retiring, and then living off savings.

"Many of our clients envision a transition period that might include part-time work, consulting, caregiving, starting a business, or spending more time supporting children and grandchildren," Glenn told Yahoo Finance.

The HSBC survey found the most common priorities among affluent individuals were personal or professional reinvention (52%), such as changing careers or pursuing a new passion, followed by retirement and supporting the next generation (both 38%).

There is no one-size-fits-all savings goal . One common guideline is to aim for 10 to 12 times your annual salary by retirement, according to Fidelity Investments, though your target may be higher or lower. You can also calculate retirement savings needs by age .

Glenn said headlines touting a million or more in retirement savings may mislead savers.

"People can get into trouble when they treat a retirement target as a magic number instead of a thoughtful planning process. The real question is: What kind of life are you trying to fund?"

Glenn said it's more important to determine how much capital might be needed to support a particular vision of retirement — whether that includes travel, philanthropy, or helping family members.

"The starting point should be your expected spending, not the size of your portfolio. The goal isn't to hit someone else's number," she added.

articles.title: SpaceX, Tesla stocks tumble as Democratic sweep raises questions on merger prospects, AI build-out
articles.summary: SpaceX and Tesla extended declines on Thursday.
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) stocks extended declines on Thursday, each dropping roughly 9%. Shares of the Elon Musk-led companies were pounded after Democrats won control of the House and Senate this week, raising concerns over regulatory hurdles for data center buildouts in the US and merger aspirations between the two companies.

The Democratic win in Texas, where both SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered, is at the center of the concern. The state flipped blue at the gubernatorial level and saw the Senate seat won by James Talarico, with whom Musk got into fierce spats on social media leading up to the elections.

"We will believe a SpaceX/Tesla merger happens but now faces a much tougher regulatory roadmap to get this deal done in 2027 given this new political blue roadmap in DC/Texas," Yorkville's partner and managing director Dan Ives wrote on Thursday.

Elon Musk said on SpaceX's third quarter earnings call last month that he thinks merging the company with Tesla ( TSLA ) would be a good idea and revealed that both companies are exploring a potential deal.

Earlier this year, Musk also announced the launch of a Terafab, a massive semiconductor manufacturing complex in Texas that would supply SpaceX and Tesla.

Worries over a slowdown in data center build-outs also dampened shares of Texas-based SpaceX, which has increasingly leaned into AI compute as a revenue source.

Ives said while Big Tech and hyperscaler capex should still easily exceed $1 trillion in 2027, the growth rate into 2028 "will clearly moderate significantly as the data center buildout comes at a much slower pace given the political map, especially in the state of Texas."

On Wednesday, Goldman Sachs analysts also calculated, "Democratic wins at the state and local level are likely to lead to short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion.

articles.title: Lyft Launches $9.99-a-Month Program With DoorDash Membership
articles.summary: Lyft Inc. is launching a new loyalty program that includes a DoorDash Inc. membership and credits toward future rides or delivery orders, setting it up to be...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Lyft Inc. ( LYFT ) is launching a new loyalty program that includes a DoorDash Inc. ( DASH ) membership and credits toward future rides or delivery orders, setting it up to better compete with rival Uber Technologies Inc.'s subscription offering.

The Lyft Go With DashPass program gives riders 8% back in the form of credits that can be used toward future trips or DoorDash orders, according to a statement Thursday. The plan costs $9.99 a month, or $96 yearly, and replaces a similarly priced Lyft Pink membership. Current members will be transferred to the new one automatically at no charge.

Notably, the new Lyft Go membership won't include any free access to bikes and scooters that Lyft operates, such as Citi Bike in the New York area. The existing Lyft Pink All Access tier, which will remain an annual $199 subscription, will be the only program that will offer free unlocks and other bike and scooter perks.

Lyft is also offering a $4.99 monthly loyalty option. Dubbed Lyft Go Core, it will offer 5% back in credits redeemable on rides.

The move represents a deepening partnership between Lyft and DoorDash, which have teamed up since 2024 in offering discounts for their respective services. Uber has pointed to subscriptions as an important engine of financial growth: The 55 million members of the Uber One subscription contribute to more than half of that company's total gross bookings, the ride-hailing giant said during earnings remarks on Wednesday.

Since Lyft doesn't operate a food delivery service, adding a DoorDash membership that waives delivery fees could make a Lyft program more comparable to an Uber One subscription, and attract ridership.

Uber One, which is also $9.99 a month, offers 5% back on rides in the form of Uber credits, zero delivery fee and discounts on orders.

articles.title: US weekly jobless claims at 57-year lows; worker productivity surges in third quarter
articles.summary: By Lucia Mutikani WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits slipped to a 57-year low last week, point...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 5 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits slipped to a 57-year low last week, pointing to labor market resilience, though uncertainty over the drawn-out conflict in the Middle East is constraining hiring.

Other data from the Labor Department on Thursday showed stronger-than-expected growth in worker productivity in the third quarter. The surge in productivity depressed labor costs for the ‌first time in more than a year and reinforced views of policymakers and economists that the labor market was not a source of inflation.

Benign wage inflation gives the Federal Reserve more latitude to focus on ‌rising price pressures stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran. Anger over the conflict, now in its ninth month, cost President Donald Trump's Republican party control of Congress, with Democrats performing strongly in this week's midterm elections.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 189,000 for ​the week ended October 31, the Labor Department said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 196,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims matched the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, which was the lowest reading since 1969. They have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September. Low layoffs, thanks to strong domestic demand and profit growth, are anchoring the labor market. But some economists viewed the low level of jobless claims as a function of a smaller labor force amid an immigration crackdown, rather than fewer job cuts.

Others believed the labor market could be tightening. The government reported this week that there were 1.06 open jobs for every unemployed person in September, up from 1.02 in August.

No state reported an increase in unadjusted claims in excess of 1,000 last week. A separate ‌report from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas showed US-based employers announced 43,994 ⁠job cuts in October, up 2% from September. Planned layoffs dropped 71% compared to October 2025.

Despite the rise over the month, layoffs were the lowest for any October since 2023. Employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers last month, a 57% jump from October 2025. Hiring plans were the highest for any October since 2009, and likely mostly seasonal jobs.

"Employers are holding on ⁠to the workers they have heading into the holidays, and the hiring they are announcing is largely short-term, seasonal work," said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. "Companies want the flexibility to meet holiday demand without adding permanent headcount."

articles.title: Thicker bacon and ditching breakfast. Wendy’s hopes a menu shakeup can revive sales
articles.summary: Wendy’s reported its seventh consecutive quarter of declining sales, prompting the company to reveal a turnaround plan while rejecting a massive takeover offer.
articles.body: Wendy’s reported its seventh consecutive quarter of declining sales, prompting the company to reveal a turnaround plan while rejecting a massive takeover offer. Thursday’s earnings caps off a tumultuous period for the 56-year-old chain, which included hundreds of closures, leadership changes and slumping sales. Wendy’s has been battling a number of issues that hurt its bottom line, including consumers cutting back on dining out, higher beef prices and value offerings that aren’t bringing people in. Same-store sales at its US locations fell 5.7% for the third quarter ending on September 27. Wendy’s sales trails its chief rivals, including McDonald’s, which fell 0.2%, and a reinvigorated Burger King, who reported an 8.4% increase. The multi-year turnaround plan, dubbed “Dave’s Way” after Wendy’s founder Dave Thomas, will include improvements to the food, better marketing and expanded delivery. CEO Bob Wright on Thursday said that its “objective is clear: grow customer traffic and market share while strengthening restaurant profitability.” At the same time, the chain’s board announced that it “unanimously rejected” a $1.4 billion offer from a group of investors, including former chairman and largest shareholder Nelson Peltz, to buy Wendy’s and take it private. The company said the offer undervalues Wendy’s and its potential. “Our confidence rests firmly in Bob Wright’s proven track record of seasoned industry leadership, including restaurant business turnarounds,” said Art Winkleblack, Wendy’s board chair and a member of the independent committee, in a statement. What’s next Wendy’s new plan will improve the food, with a “fully refreshed menu” rolling out in 2027. Wright has previously criticized that the chain had prioritized cost savings over the quality of the food. The chain is starting with the ingredients – thicker bacon, bigger pieces of lettuce for sandwiches, creamier Frosty’s and upgraded salads. Wright said that the chain is also “removing lower volume items that add complexity in our kitchens.” One major part of the menu that could go away is breakfast, which Wendy’s launched in 2020. The company is now making it optional for franchisees. Locations that have stopped selling it report better results during other parts of the day. “This option directly supports stronger restaurant economics, improves the employee experience and importantly allows operators to concentrate on the food offerings and day parts,” Wright said. Wendy’s woes Over the past several months, Wendy’s has shuttered nearly 300 of its 6,000 restaurants across the United States that were “consistently underperforming. This was the second wave of substantial closures within two years, part of the chain’s efforts to boost profits at nearby locations. In May, Wendy’s appointed Wright as its chief executive officer, ending a nearly year-long leadership drought after previous CEO Kirk Tanner left for Hershey after just 18 months with the chain. Wright’s record of growing sandwich chain Potbelly was likely seen attractive to Wendy’s board, considering same-store sales have fallen for six consecutive quarters. The new CEO was blunt during his first earnings call in August, saying the chain was “not performing at our potential.” Notably, Wendy’s let rival Burger King surpass it in US sales this year, knocking it down to the country’s third-biggest burger chain. “Our value proposition has slipped, and franchisee economics are under pressure,” Wright previously said. “I’ve seen this brand at its best, and I know we can fix these issues.” Wendy’s struggles have also adversely affected a major franchisee, Meritage Hospitality Group, which operates more than 300 US locations and partially blamed its bankruptcy on Wendy’s slumping sales. The franchise group said that its store-level earnings nosedived nearly 50% last year, citing rising beef costs, increased discounting and weak traffic. Wendy’s announced that it was planning acquiring “up to” 163 locations from the group, unless they receive a better offer. Wendy’s has unveiled transformation plans in the past, prompting an analyst on the call to ask what’s different about this version. Wright said that, compared to previous plans, franchisees are behind this one. “The restaurant business is deceptively simple to understand,” Wright said. “Writing a strategy that makes sense is the easy part. It’s unbelievably difficult to execute, and it requires that that execution strength across all disciplines.”

articles.title: Qualcomm, Micron, Sandisk, and AMD stocks sink, leading chip sector lower
articles.summary: Qualcomm, Micron, and Arm Holdings were all trading lower on Thursday as chip stocks continued to slide.
articles.body:
Chip stocks sank on Thursday, extending declines from the prior session, with Qualcomm ( QCOM ), Micron Technology ( MU ), Sandisk ( SDNK ), and AMD ( AMD ) falling by double-digit percentages. Despite a broader market rally on Wednesday following Democrats' midterm election victory, semiconductor stocks moved lower amid the threat that stricter regulation could slow data center construction.

Semiconductor stocks, which drove the AI trade higher this year, have been volatile since the summer. The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) fell by 8%, trimming the index's year-to-date gains to roughly 30%.

The declines were led by Qualcomm, which issued an underwhelming profit forecast , signaling that higher-cost components are weighing on the smartphone processor maker.

Shares of Arm Holdings ( ARM ) also fell after the chip designer issued revenue guidance that, while slightly above consensus, failed to impress investors who priced in a higher range amid the AI boom.

Micron Technology stock also declined after the memory chipmaker paused plans for a Taiwanese plant due to labor disputes. Sandisk slid 15%, extending declines from 7% in the prior session.

SK Hynix ( SKHY ) was also trading lower in premarket trading after shares of the South Korean memory maker tumbled overseas, alongside Samsung Electronics ( 005930.K S ).

At the same time, shares of US chipmaker Intel ( INTC ) declined nearly 5%, while AMD plunged 12%. Nvidia ( NVDA ) also extended declines from the prior session.

articles.title: Stock market today: Nasdaq plunges 5% as chip stocks sell off, Dow and S&P 500 give back post-election rally gains
articles.summary: US stock futures split as the crosscurrents of a power shift in Washington, the war in Iran, earnings, and labor market data overlapped.
articles.body: US stocks fell suddenly on Thursday as AI and chip stocks sold off, erasing the gains from Wednesday’s post-election rally.The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) tumbled 2.2%, or over 1,200 points. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) fell 3.3%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) dropped 5%, putting the index on track to close in a correction.The PHLX Semiconductor index (^SOX) dived 11% as Nvidia (NVDA), Micron (MU), and other chip names sank.Investors continued to process the Democrats' sweeping victory on Tuesday and its implications for markets and the economy. Amid relief that election uncertainty has been removed, the stock market continues to sort out the perceived winners and losers of a regime change on Capitol Hill.Oil prices rose amid uncertainty that President Trump would pursue a deal with Iran to end the war in the Middle East. Optimism grew overnight after Vice President JD Vance said, "The reason we lost [the midterm elections] is the war," in a post on X suggesting the party should push for a resolution to the conflict. Brent crude oil (BZ=F) prices traded around $97 per barrel, while US benchmark WTI crude (CL=F) stood at $90 per barrel.A report from Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoff plans in October fell to the lowest level since 2023 as companies turned their attention to retaining existing employees, setting the scene for Friday's key employment report.On the earnings calendar, Duke Energy (DUK), Airbnb (ABNB), and Lumentum (LITE), among others, report results.
